purpose: Larotrectinib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain solid tumors in adults and children that have a specific gene change called an NTRK fusion. It works regardless of where the cancer is in the body, as long as that gene change is present. Your doctor will do a special test to confirm your cancer has this gene change before starting this medicine.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells have an abnormal protein called a TRK fusion protein that tells them to grow out of control. Larotrectinib works like a lock-and-key — it blocks that abnormal protein and stops it from signaling cancer cells to keep growing. By targeting this specific change, it can shrink or slow down the cancer with less harm to normal, healthy cells compared to traditional chemotherapy.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, constipation, feeling unsteady or having balance problems, muscle or joint pain, and elevated liver enzymes (found on blood tests). Most side effects are mild to moderate.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious nervous system problems like confusion, memory issues, difficulty speaking, or problems with balance and walking — tell your doctor right away if you notice these. It can harm an unborn baby, so do not become pregnant or father a child during treatment. Avoid grapefruit and certain other medicines that can affect how this drug works in your body. Your doctor will monitor your liver with regular blood tests.
typical_dosing: For adults and children weighing 50 kg (about 110 lbs) or more, the usual dose is 100 mg taken by mouth twice a day. For smaller children, the dose is based on body surface area (calculated from height and weight) and is also taken twice a day. It can be taken with or without food. Capsules should be swallowed whole; an oral liquid solution is available for those who cannot swallow capsules.
